title: The Week That Was
text:
Athena Smith

Meet The Authors

Subscribe to Lawfare

On Lawfare Daily, Benjamin Wittes, Molly Roberts, Eric Columbus, Roger Parloff, and Anna Bower sat down to discuss the latest litigation over Trump administration policies, including updates on Trump’s beautification projects, a judge’s rejection of the BBC’s motion to dismiss Trump’s defamation suit, the Fourth Circuit’s ruling blocking a DOJ demand for journalists’ LinkedIn data, the D.C. Circuit’s decision protecting U.S. Agency for Global Media head Michael Abramowitz from removal, and more.On Lawfare Daily, Julia Curlee sat down with Chris McGuire to discuss the spy scandal that forced out Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. The two covered how advanced Nvidia chips reached Chinese AI labs through Megaspeed, a Singapore company once run by suspected Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang, why the Commerce Department never cut off the flow of chips, what China gained, and more.Michael Feinberg unpacked the common misconceptions surrounding honey traps—seduction or sexual relationships used to gather intelligence—and suggested that they can be used as a routine part of the recruitment process.  Feinberg explained that honey traps rarely employ blackmail because the emotional attachment of the relationship, not a one-time threat, is what gives these connections their potency and usefulness for intelligence gathering.On Lawfare Live, on Friday, Nov. 20, at 4 p.m. ET, Wittes spoke with Roberts, Parloff, and Bower to discuss the latest litigation over Trump administration policies, including updates on Trump’s monuments, the “grand conspiracy” investigation, attacks on law firms, and more.On Lawfare Daily, Feinberg sat down with Nick Harkaway to discuss one of spy fiction’s most indelible characters: George Smiley. The two covered fact and fiction in the world of spy novels, Harkaway’s new book, “The Taper Man: A Novel of John le Carré's Circus,” and more. On Rational Security, Scott Anderson spoke with Roberts, Bower, and Feinberg to cover the past week’s various outages and communications issues, how the Trump administration may fight back against Democratic oversight efforts in January’s new Congress, the brawl inside the Trump administration following the Nvidia scandal, and more.Lisa Klaassen detailed how company stakes are calculated bids by the U.S. government for leverage over strategic industries. Klaassen noted that this approach raises risks because the government is purchasing stakes in the same firms it regulates. She argued that the government can just as easily cut off these companies and that America's competitive edge derives from fostering market competition with minimal intervention.On Lawfare Daily, Daniel Byman sat down with John Donnelly to discuss Donnelly’s new book, “Lifeline: The Story of PEPFAR, the Greatest Humanitarian Initiative of Our Time.” The two spoke about the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), the Bush administration’s landmark effort to fight AIDS in Africa; the origins of the program; how its architects overcame political and bureaucratic obstacles; and whether the United States still has the ability to change the world for good.Hady Amr noted that Americans flying to Tel Aviv are increasingly denied entry by Israel, possibly because of their political expression. Amr described how denials generally fall into two categories: Palestinian Americans denied entry to the West Bank or Americans denied entry to Israel due to their political views. Amr emphasized that reciprocity in visa privileges is a requirement of U.S. law which the U.S. should enforce.On Lawfare Daily, Mykhailo Soldatenko sat down with Serhii Plokhy to discuss Plokhy’s new book, "Killing the Pope," which tells the history of an attempted assassination of Pope John Paul II during the Cold War and unpacks the investigations, trials, and propaganda battles that ensued. Catherine Grace Katz contended that the proposed trilateral meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping on the sidelines of November’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit in Shenzhen can be accurately described as a second Yalta Conference. Katz detailed how the White House’s support for Ukraine appears to be running dry, and just as the original Yalta conference indicated Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s sell out of Eastern Europe to Stalin, the U.S. could indicate disregard for Ukrainian sovereignty.Jay Atanda warned that the U.S. lacks a standard protocol for identifying biological material, leaving it exposed to a web of systemic biosecurity vulnerabilities. Atanda outlined how artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled biological design tools pose novel threats alongside the dangers caused by accidents in research labs or legitimate researchers circumventing rules. He concluded that the U.S. government should move proactively, creating a federal agency and a database to coordinate interdiction and testing.Samuel Morse argued that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit is likely to vacate an earlier panel’s decision upholding the Pentagon’s blacklisting of Anthropic. Morse noted that in three recent cases implicating questions of executive power, the en banc D.C. Circuit reversed 2-1 decisions which favored executive power. He also highlighted that a reversal may send the case to the Supreme Court.Scott Shapiro detailed how computer scientists have used formal logic to find security issues in software and how that same process of finding loopholes can be applied to legal rules such as contracts and tax code. Shapiro explained—using a tax law solver as an example—the process by which solvers can hunt for legal loopholes, optimize strategies, or prove that no loophole exists before putting rules into effect.Sam Bresnick and Emelia Probasco described how the use of artificial intelligence decision-making support systems (AI DSS) has the potential to make attacks on data more dangerous. Bresnick and Probasco laid out how the use of AI in analytical methods opens up the risk of bad data—which may be increasingly manipulated by foreign countries—and could pressure analysts to make faster decisions. The authors recommended that the U.S. expand its capacity to check for and catch accidents.Tom Uren analyzed the Trump administration’s AI task force’s decision to encourage regulatory agencies to go easy on organizations targeted by AI cyberattacks. He also described the Commerce Department’s new AI regulations tightening controls on who can buy AI chips, why as-is these restrictions will likely not keep Nvidia chips out of China’s AI labs, and more.Ziad Reslan, Kim Malfacini, and Kevin Chen argued generative artificial intelligence (AI) may become necessary for full participation in society, requiring consideration of the technology as a right. The authors detailed that this evolution creates serious implications for how developers should approach user policy and that a right to AI could have both negative and aspirational dimensions.Cullen O’Keefe and Charlie Winter argued that the chains of thought (CoT) used in frontier artificial intelligence (AI) reasoning should be transparent in order to encourage AI deployment safety and build an understanding of AI safety failures. O’Keefe and Winter recommended that AI companies develop a more formal consensus for minimal CoT monitorability and only commit to advancing AI capabilities if monitoring remains intact.On Scaling Laws, Kevin Frazier met with Alex Bores and Alexandra Reeve Givens to analyze what a staggering midterm win for Democrats means for AI policy, the significance of President Trump’s change in Chief of Staff for how local officials may act on AI, the specific policy issues that seem likely to receive broad support, and more.And that was the week that was.
